feedback: Written before this candidate has raced, so it makes no claim about its result. Iteration 2 (y=0.07 with a shorter, lighter body) fell to 47.8 and lost s-bend progress (0.163 to 0.119). That run changed two things at once, so it does not show the lead effect alone, but it is the only evidence on the forward direction. Iterations 5 and 6 showed that larger wheel_radius (41.4) and higher mass (42.7) both cut s-bend progress, and iteration 7 (wheel_radius 0.025 m) scored 57.9, so the controller and geometry are close to a local optimum at radius 0.03 m, mass 0.8 kg and wheel_track 0.08 m. I kept the iteration 4 controller so that the y change is the only variable. When the next race reports: if s-bend and slalom progress hold at or above 0.185 and max_error or steering_oscillation falls, the shorter lead is helping, so try a further step. If line_loss_events rise on the s-bend or slalom, or progress falls, the lead is too short for the sharpest bends, so return to y=0.05 m.
requested_changes: If progress holds at or above 0.185 and max_error falls on the s-bend and slalom with line loss at or below iteration 4: try y=0.02 m with the same span and 16 mm footprints. Evidence: iteration 4 (y=0.05) gave max_error 0.0656 on the s-bend, pinned at the floor, and iteration 2 (y=0.07) hurt, so the shorter direction is the one still open.

If line_loss_events rise above about 1.0 on the slalom or s-bend, return y to 0.05 m and try sensor_size 0.012 at that height instead. Evidence: iteration 1 to 4 showed line loss falls as the sensor span widens, and iteration 4 already has 0.95 line loss on the s-bend, so a shorter lead may need more coverage per sensor.
Keep wheel_track 0.08 m, wheel_radius 0.03 m and mass 0.8 kg unchanged. Evidence: iterations 5, 6 and 7 each moved one of these and scored 41.4, 42.7 and 57.9 against 58.5 for iteration 4.
